deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It is a set of reading excerpts headed 'Causalität', copied in Riemann's hand from J. F. Herbart's Sämmtliche Werke (Hartenstein edition). The previous page excerpts Locke's Essay on liberty and the will; the next continues with Herbart on Fichte, the 'Intension' of the Ich, and Herbart's Psychologie.

(1) Herbart, Werke Bd. 3, p. 206 (Allgemeine Metaphysik I, §194).
- If the real (das Reale) is thought of as a ground whose essence is to ground something, then before its consequence it becomes a mere possibility of becoming. If no becoming developed from it, it would not be what it is, and so would not be at all.
- Herbart's opposite view: the real is complete in itself ('in sich reif') and needs no development. Happening (Geschehen) adds nothing to it.
- The phrase 'it comes in addition' must not be read as an addition. One does not add lines to surfaces, or surfaces to bodies. Likewise happening cannot be added to the real, because the two are entirely heterogeneous. The only quasi-mathematical content is this analogy with the non-additivity of magnitudes of different dimension.
- Kant is right that 'Sein ist bloß die Position eines Dinges', but the posited thing must stand by itself without needing anything further, either as consequence or as ground.
- Spinoza and the older school wrongly multiply 'realities' in a causa immanens in proportion to its power, that is, its potential consequences. The etymology of existentia, actualitas and Wirklichkeit betrays the error that being shows itself only in acting.

(2) Herbart, p. 208.
- Kant reduced causality to a rule of temporal succession supplied by the understanding.
- Against this: beneath apparent happening there must be a real happening, at least the genesis of our representations and the acts of freedom.

(3) Herbart, p. 209.
- Real happening is an inner happening. It cannot float free of the real. It is tied to the real as a surface is tied to its body.
- Hence it shares in the timelessness of the real. Temporal order (earlier and later) applies only when happenings are compared with one another, not to the real as their ground.

(4) Herbart, p. 211. Ontology must clarify the concept of a thing as bearer of essential and accidental marks. This task coincides with explaining real happening.

(5) Herbart's annotations (1796) to Schelling's 'Vom Ich als Princip der Philosophie oder über das Unbedingte im menschlichen Wissen', Werke XII, 35.
- Schelling's three acts of the Ich are: absolute self-positing, limitation, and striving against the limitation.
- These yield no transition into change. Time is posited only problematically. The 'Gegeneinanderstreben' is anything but change, and must not be thought in time, any more than the pure concept of causality is (reference to Jacobi, 'Über den transcendentalen Idealismus' / David Hume über den Glauben, oder Idealismus und Realismus).
- Then a Fichte remark begins: time arises only in reflection and is merely a form of intuition. It continues on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible: the page contains no computation. The excerpts closely follow Herbart's text. The Kant dictum 'Sein ist bloß die Position eines Dinges' is correctly attributed (Einzig möglicher Beweisgrund 1763; KrV A598/B626).

results.what: Excerpt of Herbart's critique of causality as 'ground' and of the additivity of happening to the real, with the analogy that lines cannot be added to surfaces nor surfaces to bodies.
results.modern_name: Herbartian realism / ontology of 'Reale' and 'Geschehen'; dimensional heterogeneity as an analogy.

results.what: Excerpt of Herbart's 1796 objections to Schelling's 'Vom Ich': no transition from absolute positing to change, so time is merely problematic.
results.modern_name: Early Herbart critique of Fichte and Schelling.

results.what: Riemann's study of Herbart in his philosophical notes.
results.usually_credited_to: Well documented: Riemann's Nachlass, Dedekind/Weber edition 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts'; Scholz 1982

deep.surprise_reason: These are verbatim reading notes from Herbart's works. Riemann's intensive study of Herbart is well known (he himself declared himself a Herbartian in epistemology, though not in natural philosophy). The page contains no original mathematics.
transcription_corrections: 'p. 209 ... dass ein wirkliches Geschehen ist eingewendet worden' — the image and Herbart's sense suggest 'eingeräumt worden' (conceded), not 'eingewendet'.
'Das Gegeneinanderstreben ist nichts als [-T-] T weniger als Wechsel' should read 'ist nichts weniger als Wechsel'. 'als' is struck through and 'T' is an insertion mark.
'im Jahr 1796.' at the left margin is more likely 'v. Jahre 1796' (vom Jahre 1796), dating Herbart's annotations.
'Man möge[?] es' at p. 211 looks like 'Man mag es'.
'Begriff der Substanz[?]' at p. 211: the image reading is uncertain. Herbart's text speaks of the concept of the thing (Ding/Dinges) as bearer of marks; the word may be 'des Dinges'.
'mit der übrigen[?]' is likely 'mit der übrigen' or 'mit der andern'; uncertain.
'die Erscheinung[?] der Eigenschaften[?]' is uncertain; it possibly reads 'die Scheinbarkeit' or similar.
